_note: Passages where Shaykh Ibrāhīm DEFINES a term rather than construing a verse. The verse index answers 'what did he say about this āya'; this answers 'what did he mean by this word'. Keyed to the same loci, so a definition always carries its page and its date.

links.glossEn: A verse has a ẓāhir and a bāṭin like other verses — stated as a general principle of reading, then applied to give al-samāʾ both a figurative sense (rain) and a real one.
Taqwā outward and inward: compliance with the command and avoidance of the prohibition in the manner that pleases. Before jadhb it is a veil; after it, perfection.

A tajallī among the tajalliyāt of al-Ḥaqq which gathers all the rest; the Garden and its fifteen worlds are a tajallī of the quṭb, who himself draws from the Seal and beyond that from the Muḥammadan ḥaqīqa.

The aqṭāb are many; the Fard is one in each age, and from him the ʿārifūn of that age draw supply. Unqualified, 'quṭb' means the comprehensive one — but the word is also used of anyone on whom a station or a state turns.
The driving out of the siwā in one's dealing with al-Ḥaqq — and therefore possible only for the one who has maʿrifa, since whoever knows the other-than-Him has not the strength for it.
A ḥāl that comes over the firmly established ʿārif through the witnessing of Greatness. Opposite to uns, as qabḍ is opposite to basṭ and fear to hope.
The maʿārif of the maʿārif, and equally the rising higher. Its way is unbroken pondering of the relations between rubūbiyya and ʿubūdiyya, and nothing else.
Creation's nearness to al-Ḥaqq is their being brought to nothing in His existence. The Prophet's drawing-near is not that: it is real, with his noble essence remaining.
That God's oneness is not the oneness of numerical scarcity found among created things, but a unity to which all multiplicities return.
links.quotedFrom: Abū Muḥammad al-Amīr, by way of Muḥammad ʿIllīsh's fatāwā
